1.pericope_label: Darius orders the search; the roll of Cyrus is found at Achmetha, with its warrant for the house, its charges and its vessels

schools.summary: Gill makes the order an inquiry after the edict among the public records, rejects for a place-name the reading that took Achmetha for a vessel in which writings were kept, follows the Vulgate and Josephus in Ecbatana and explains the Persian summer and winter residences, and passes on the reading that makes the three rows the walls and the great stones marble.

Henry reads the search as a trap that failed, the adversaries appealing to a decree they hoped would not be found and the tribes having kept no copy to plead; he credits Darius with refusing to treat the absence of the roll at Babylon as proof that no decree existed, suspects that someone unwilling to destroy it had hidden it out of ill will, and sorts the recovered document into three warrants, noting that the promised money seems never to have arrived.

Clarke renders the house of the rolls the house of the books, that is the royal library, and remarks that this is the first mention of a library at all; he measures the new house against Solomon and finds it much the larger, and notes that Cyrus charged himself with the timber and the sacrifices while the Jews paid the rest. Wesley traces the two stages of the search and refuses the comparison with Solomon so stated, offering either a difference of cubits or a reference to the porch alone.

Ellicott corrects the wording in two places, order for decree and laid down for laid up, and alone explains why a transcript rather than the original was found; he reads the strengthened foundation clause and the return of the vessels as expiation for Belshazzar. Delitzsch supposes the Babylon search itself disclosed where the Cyrus documents were kept, gives the fullest account of Achmetha, and notes the distributive singular that sends each vessel to its own place.

debates.question: What was Achmetha, and why was the roll there?

sides.position: a place, namely Ecbatana, the Median summer residence of the Persian kings, against the reading that made it a vessel for storing writings
the capital of Great Media built by Dejokes, near the modern Hamadan, with Achmetha the Old-Median form of the name
the original parchment was probably destroyed at Babylon, so that only a transcript survived to be found here
someone unwilling to destroy the decree hid it there out of ill will, that the Jews might lose its benefit

debates.question: How do the decreed dimensions stand against Solomon temple?

sides.position: much larger, sixty cubits each way against twenty broad and thirty high
the comparison cannot stand so: either Solomon cubits were sacred and larger, or the sixty cubits of height belong to the porch only

outliers: Clarke alone remarks that the house of the books is the first library we hear of.
Ellicott alone finds every word of the clause about the vessels emphatic, down to the twice-repeated house of God.
themes: a decree searched for and found elsewhere
a copy that outlived its original
charges laid on a royal revenue
vessels sent back each to its own place

6.pericope_label: The decree of Darius: the officers to keep clear, the charges and sacrifices to be supplied, and a curse on whoever alters the word

schools.summary: Gill places the governor on the Israel side of the Euphrates, hears in the phrasing a suspicion that the officers meant to molest the builders, parts company with Josephus by taking this for an additional decree granting more than Cyrus had, and reads the closing clause of the Shechinah dwelling as in Solomon temple.

Clarke turns the warning off into a positive charge to further the work, draws out the policy by which even heathens thought offerings made on their behalf would avail and states with an established religion have tolerated others for the benefit of their prayers, and canvasses the punishments before settling on empaling. Wesley turns the curse forward onto the Romans, who as instruments of the temple later destruction perhaps felt it in the decline of their empire.

Ellicott marks the abrupt turn into the words of the decree, allows that its terms were either drawn with Jewish help or rendered into the national phraseology, traces the money to tribute already collected, argues that the word for sweet savours means incense and shows under what good instruction the decree was drawn, and reports that the penalty named is literally crucifixion. Delitzsch summarises the whole as promotion rather than permission, observes that the written answer is given without being announced as such, and sets the closing imprecation beside the Persian inscription at Bisitun.

debates.question: Is this an additional decree or a confirmation of Cyrus?

sides.position: an additional decree of Darius granting more than Cyrus had, against the older view that it was no more than a confirmation of the earlier one

debates.question: Why does a Persian king provide for Israelite sacrifice?

sides.position: two ends are served, the honouring of the God of heaven and the interceding of the Jews for the dynasty

Darius walks in the footsteps of Cyrus, who owned the God of Israel as the God of heaven; the acknowledgment cost a Persian king nothing, since he might honour Jahve as mightiest without renouncing his fathers gods
policy rather than theology: even heathens believed such offerings would avail, and states have tolerated other religions for the benefit of their prayers

debates.question: What penalty does the decree threaten?

sides.position: literally crucifixion, among the Persians nailing to a cross after decapitation and among the Assyrians impalement
which punishment is meant is not clear; empaling seems intended, and the house is to be left rubble fit only for sordid uses

outliers: Delitzsch alone sets the closing imprecation beside the end of the Bisitun inscription, where a god judgments are called down on whoever defaces the image and the writing.
Ellicott alone argues that the connection with the prayer proves the sweet savours to be incense.
Wesley alone extends the curse to the Romans who destroyed the temple at last.
themes: adversaries ordered to keep their distance
a pagan revenue charged with a daily sacrifice
prayer for the dynasty written into a decree
a curse borrowed from royal Persian form

13.pericope_label: The work prospers and the house is finished in the sixth year of Darius; the dedication, the twelve he-goats, and the ministry set in order

schools.summary: Gill fixes Adar as the twelfth month, calls the dedication offerings hecatombs of a kind reckoned grand even among heathens and such as Homer speaks of, distinguishes burnt from peace offerings and the offerers feast upon their part, reads the children of Israel as Judah and Benjamin with some of the ten tribes mixed, and has the priests and Levites set in their proper classes to serve in turn.

Henry makes the reversal the point, that the men who had hurried to stop the work now hurried to help it and did the king bidding speedily so as not to seem grudging, their moderation forced on them by his; and he has the elders build cheerfully and perhaps with their own hands.

Clarke dates the finishing by years of the world and turns the three kings into a chronology of favour, God giving the first order and stirring up each king after to second it; he reads the he-goats as a sin offering for every tribe and marks the end of the Aramaic section at the last verse. Wesley supplies the caution that the success was not chance nor the king good humour but God, who required the work by his prophets and disposed the royal heart.

Ellicott dates the completion to the last month of the ecclesiastical year and reckons both intervals, takes the verse naming the kings as a summary of every agent in the work, infers from the one royal title that Ezra writes in the reign of the later Artaxerxes, presses the twelve goats as marking all Israel, and warns that only the general arrangements of the ministry stood in the law. Delitzsch states the chronological difficulty of the third name plainly, and reads the twelve as answering to the tribes because the temple was meant for the whole covenant people.

debates.question: How long did the building take?

sides.position: four years five months and ten days from the resumption, but twenty-one years from the first foundation
twenty years after Zerubbabel laid the foundation under Cyrus

debates.question: Why is Artaxerxes named with Cyrus and Darius?

sides.position: a predecessor of Darius cannot be meant by a later name, so it must be Longimanus, who reigned long after the temple was finished
the verse is a summary of every agent in the work, and the royal title given to him alone shows Ezra writing in his reign and adding the name
the writer is recapitulating the sovereigns who favoured the Jews after the captivity

debates.question: Why twelve he-goats for a people returned from two tribes?

sides.position: because the temple was meant for the whole covenant people, whose return the prophets taught them to hope for, and not because families of the ten tribes were among the returned
because the worshippers are now called all Israel, and only here is a kid brought for each tribe
because those of the ten tribes who remained, or who came back with the Jews, were in the company

outliers: Gill alone compares the dedication offerings to the hecatombs of heathen sacrifice that Homer speaks of.
Clarke alone marks the seam where the Aramaic part of the chapter ends.
Ellicott alone warns that the restoration of the courses must have been imperfect, with neither the priestly courses complete nor the Levites in full force.
themes: hinderers turned into helpers by a royal word
a house finished to the day
a sin offering counted by tribes long scattered
an order of ministry restored imperfectly

19.pericope_label: The children of the captivity keep the passover and the feast of unleavened bread with joy, for the LORD had turned the heart of the king

schools.summary: Gill names the month Nisan or Abib and notes the feast kept at the precise time the law commanded, has the ministers pure to a man and purified as one man with the dispatch of a single man, sees Judah and Benjamin with some of the ten tribes in the company, and marks the feast of unleavened bread following immediately on the passover.

Clarke argues from the law that no second passover was needed since all were ready at once, takes those who separated themselves for gentile proselytes won by the example of the captives, and follows Calmet in reading Assyria for Persia, adding what he knows of Darius character and his marriage to two daughters of Cyrus. Wesley thinks the company drawn from each of the twelve tribes and keeps the emphasis on the God who gave them both cause and hearts to rejoice.

Ellicott notes the return to Hebrew at this celebration and reads the occasion as a renewal of the redemption from Egypt, repunctuates the verse on the purifying against the received accentuation, denies outright that proselytes from the heathen are meant, and takes the week of unleavened bread as the symbol of entire separation to the God accepted at the passover. Delitzsch counts only a few weeks from the dedication, reads the note on purity as explaining how the feast could be kept at all, and locates the turning of the king heart in the strengthening of their hands.

debates.question: Who are those that had separated themselves?

sides.position: proselytes from the heathen, gentiles who embraced the Jewish religion through mixing with the captives
not proselytes at all, but the remnant of Jews left in the land who had consorted with the populations the conquerors introduced

debates.question: Who made up the company that kept the feast?

sides.position: Judah and Benjamin with some of the ten tribes mixed among them
probably some out of each of the twelve tribes

debates.question: Why is the king called king of Assyria?

sides.position: Darius is so designated because he ruled the former realm of Assyria
Assyria stands for Persia, since Cyrus and his successors held all the rights and estates of the old Assyrian kings
the title is a remembrancer of what their oppressors had been, used pointedly to mark whose hearts God can turn

outliers: Ellicott alone observes that the Levites had by now come to slaughter all the paschal lambs.
Clarke alone draws from the proselytes the moral that a good example is persuasive when founded on pure principles.
Ellicott alone marks the change of language at this verse as Ezra returns to Hebrew.
themes: a passover kept to the day after the house was ready
a priesthood clean to a man
a question of who belonged to the congregation
the heart of an oppressor dynasty turned
